topic: Ronan Point Tower Collapse 1968: Cost-Cutting Construction Kills Sleeping Residents
niche_fit: yes - documented historical structural disaster driven by institutional negligence
_transcript: On the 16th of May, 1968, residents of Ronan  Point, a tower block in East London, were   awoken by a deafening crashing sound. Many assumed  that there had been an accident or explosion at   a nearby factory… but when they got out of bed it  was to find that the source of the sound was much   closer to home. For many residents it  was, in fact, right in their living room.  After the end of the Second World War,  Britain faced a housing deficit. Many   homes had been destroyed by German bombs during  the conflict, leaving only wasteland in their   place. As peace returned, people started raising  families once more. Especially within London,   which had been hit hard by the Blitz,  more housing was urgently needed.  One way to provide cheap and plentiful  housing was to build tower blocks. These   could be constructed quickly and relatively  cheaply, accommodated a large number of people,   and took up only a small amount of land. At the  time, tower blocks were considered an ideal,   futuristic solution to the housing deficit. Ronan Point, constructed by order of Newham   Council in 1968, was particularly cheap.  The structure, which contained 110 homes,   cost just half a million pounds, thanks  to a construction method known as Large   Panel System (or LPS) building. Using this system, large concrete   blocks and panels would be fabricated off-site,  transported in and bolted together to form the   skeleton of the building. Joints between panels  would be filled in with mortar to reinforce the   connections. Not only was this method cheap and  quick, it also required fewer skilled labourers.   The system had been pioneered in Denmark,  where it had successfully been used to   construct buildings of six-storeys or less. Of course, with the huge demand for housing in   London, taller buildings were preferred. Indeed,  the government at the time offered subsidies for   the construction of tower blocks with more  than six floors, with further subsidies for   tower blocks over fifteen or twenty floors. For this reason, Taylor Woodrow Anglian,   the construction company taken on to build  Ronan Point, used a modified version of   the of the Danish LPS method that they believed  would be suitable for much taller structures.  Thus, Ronan Point – along with several other  similar tower blocks on the same estate – was   built very quickly and on an exceptionally tight  budget. In March of 1968 families began to move   into the brand new flats. Although few residents  liked the external appearance of the building,   they were pleased with the interior.  Flats were spacious, well-equipped,   and had the luxury of central heating. They would  be ideal new homes for hundreds of Londoners.  Just two months later, on the 16th of May, 1968,  fifty-six-year-old cake decorator Ivy Hodge awoke   in her Ronan Point flat and went through to the  kitchen to prepare a cup of tea. She filled the   kettle, placed it on the stove and lit a match.  Her next step would have been to turn on the gas   supply and light it with the match… but before  she could do so she was blasted across the room   by an explosion that knocked her unconscious.  She thus did not witness what happened next.  What happened next was the almost total  destruction of her living room. The explosion   blasted out the exterior wall… the load-bearing  exterior wall. Without it in place, the wall of   the flat above had insufficient support. It  collapsed downward, as did the one above it   and the walls of two further flats above that. This material fell downward, pancaking onto the   flats below, and causing a progressive collapse  of one corner of the building that extended all   the way from Ivy Hodge’s eighteenth floor  flat to the ground floor of Ronan Point.  Almost all the flats in Ronan Point had a similar  floor plan… and thus in most cases it was the   living room of each unit that was destroyed by  the collapse, although on some floors parts of the   adjacent kitchen or bedroom were also involved.  Due to the early hour at which the collapse   took place, most residents were still in bed. Some survivors later recalled being awoken by   the deafening sound of the collapse to find the  wall of their bedroom missing, leaving nothing   between them and a sheer drop to the ground below.  In one case a woman was left stranded on a ledge   in what had previously been her living room. With  a large part of the floor having fallen away,   she could no longer reach the door, and was  forced to await rescue by emergency services.  Witnesses also recall seeing a man who,  still on top of the mattress from his bed,   was blown out of his flat and fell to  the ground several floors below. He   survived with only minor injuries, and by some  accounts did not even wake up until he landed.  Residents from all floors  of the building evacuated   down the internal stairwells. By the time the  last few arrived at the doors of Ronan Point   a crowd had gathered outside… a crowd which  applauded whenever another resident made their   escape. Survivors were taken to a local school  and offered cups of tea, and brandy. One by one,   they were painstakingly accounted for. Back at  the site, police officers searched the rubble,   equipped with polythene bags for the  body parts they expected to find.  In total, seventeen people were injured in  the collapse. Four residents were killed.   One of the injured – an eighty-two-year-old  woman – later died in hospital, albeit from   what appeared to be natural causes. In the aftermath of the collapse an   investigation was launched. It was found that  the direct trigger of the collapse had been a   gas explosion. The stove in Ivy Hodge’s flat had  been installed incorrectly, with a substandard   fitting that had been over tightened during  installation. This faulty fitting had allowed   gas to leak into the kitchen, accumulating  until a match was struck and it ignited.  This has blown out a load bearing wall,  precipitating the collapse. The government   ordered that Ronan Point be rebuilt and reinforced  so as to be able to withstand damage to a single   unit without it resulting in a progressive  collapse. Other similar tower blocks would   also be reinforced to prevent progressive  collapse. Additionally, the gas supply would be   removed from Ronan Point and the other buildings  on the estate: residents would use electricity   only for heating and cooking from that point on. The collapsed corner of Ronan Point was rebuilt,   and the building was thoroughly reinforced. In  1973, families who had been evacuated following   the collapse were invited to move back in… but  very few did so. In fact, only one elderly couple   returned to Ronan Point. New tenants were sought  for the remaining reinforced and rebuilt flats.  Some questions remained unanswered, however. The  explosion that started the collapse had been a   relatively small one. Ivy Hodge had survived. Her  hearing had not been damaged by the blast. Even   the stove itself had weathered the explosion  and remained in working order. The building   had now been reinforced against progressive  collapse, but should such a small explosion   have been able to blast out the external wall  of even a single flat in the first place?  An independent architect, Samuel Webb, developed  an interest in Ronan Point after hearing about   the disaster. Residents invited him to visit  their flats, and he conducted a series of   informal tests. He found that he could drop  a coin down behind the skirting board in one   flat and have it fall all the way through to  the flat below… something that, he surmised,   should not be the case in a soundly-constructed  building. Residents also noted that flats leaked,   and damp was a continuous problem. Some residents  even noticed cracks in their walls. Complaints to   the council would often result in small repairs  that only temporarily mitigated these issues.  Newham’s Housing Committee invited Mr Webb  to survey the whole building. Assisted by   a team of architecture students he did so, and  reported back that they had found numerous cracks   throughout the structure. He said that Ronan  Point was “beginning to break up”, and was held   up only by the reinforcements that had been made  after the public inquiry. He also noted that the   joints between concrete panels – which should have  been filled with mortar – were often filled with   nothing at all, or with wads of newspaper,  cigarette cartons and other waste material.  Further tests also revealed that the building was  vulnerable to fire. A severe fire in Ronan Point   could pass through fire doors that should contain  it for one whole hour in just eleven minutes… and   a fire of sufficient magnitude could possibly lead  to the collapse of the entire building. Indeed,   even a particularly strong storm could  also have caused the building to collapse.  These concerns, bolstered by a petition and  numerous complaints from residents, eventually   lead to the evacuation and demolition of Ronan  Point. On the day when the sign above the main   entrance was removed – the very first step in the  building’s demolition – ex-residents celebrated,   cheering and drinking champagne. They were  delighted that, after years of worry and stress,   their concerns were finally being taken  seriously, and they were being rehoused.  In addition to Ronan Point, eight other  tower blocks were also demolished. This   was a painstaking process, with the buildings  disassembled piece by piece, and architects and   other experts invited to examine the site. Samuel Webb, commented:  “I knew we were going to find bad workmanship –  what surprised me was the sheer scale of it. Not   a single joint was correct. Fixing straps were  unattached; levelling nuts were not wound down,   causing significant loading to be transmitted via  the bolts; panels were placed on bolts instead of   mortar. But the biggest shock of all was the  crucial H2 load-bearing joints between floor   and wall panels. Some of the joints had less  than fifty percent of the mortar specified.”  Ronan Point, and the other high rise buildings  on the estate were removed and replaced with   low-level housing. Ronan Point and the  estate it had been a part of had lasted,   in total, just eighteen years… when its  expected lifespan had been closer to sixty.  Though the government ordered strengthening  works be carried out on similar buildings   across the country, this wasn’t always done.  In 2017 an estate in Peckham was evacuated,   after it was found that the required remedial  works simply had not been carried out.   In 2018, an estate in Tottenham that had  been constructed using the same LPS method   as Ronan Point was evacuated, after it  was found to be structurally unsound.   Nine buildings on the estate were at risk of  collapse… and in some cases it was believed   that a collapse could have been precipitated  by an incident as minor as a car colliding   with the base of the building, or a small gas  explosion taking place in one of the flats.  The collapse of Ronan Point would not be the last  high-profile disaster to affect a government-owned   tower block in London. To this day, many  residents in such blocks live, every day,   in structures that are known or strongly  suspected to have potentially fatal flaws.
